title: Back within 12 hours with a spreading thigh rash

source.citation: Merola R, Negri C, Merola A, et al. Necrotizing Fasciitis and Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome: A Case Report. Cureus. 2024;16(11):e73917.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Worsening thigh pain and a spreading rash, now short of breath
presentation.hpi: Seen in this ED about 12 hours ago with a swollen, red, tender medial left thigh; pain there and in the groin had begun three days before the rash appeared. Ultrasound then showed marked subcutaneous thickening with a fluid layer reaching the superficial fascia. She was given ketorolac 30 mg with modest relief, declined admission and was referred to her GP. She returns with more intense pain, blood-filled blisters spreading over the medial thigh and groin, a dark hemorrhagic patch on the outer lower leg, and shortness of breath.

exam: Hemorrhagic bullae over the medial left thigh and groin
Necrotic, hemorrhagic lesion on the lateral side of the left leg

imaging.modality: Soft-tissue ultrasound of the thigh (first visit)
imaging.finding: Marked thickening of the subcutaneous tissue with a fluid layer extending to the superficial fascial planes

diagnosis.primary: Necrotizing fasciitis with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Streptococcus pyogenes)

management: Septic shock about an hour after admission to the emergency medicine ward (BP 65/40 mm Hg): intubated and given a noradrenaline infusion at 0.8 µg/kg/min
outcome: Refractory shock in the ICU, then asystole despite advanced life support; she died. Autopsy found Streptococcus pyogenes in the pleural and pericardial fluid.
teachingPoints: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, hemorrhagic bullae and skin necrosis are late signs of a necrotizing soft-tissue infection; a patient who returns within hours with worse pain after a 'cellulitis' visit has one until proven otherwise.
Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: early debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin; no debridement is reported in this case.
Fluid tracking along the fascia on ultrasound is an early clue.

questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.extra: Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL (1.3 twelve hours ago), procalcitonin 31.50 ng/mL, INR 1.74. Arterial gas: pH 7.23, PaCO2 19 mm Hg, HCO3 8.0 mmol/L, lactate 9.8 mmol/L.
options: Cellulitis with an NSAID drug reaction
questions.explanation: Rapidly spreading pain, hemorrhagic bullae and skin necrosis with tachycardia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and severe lactic acidosis point to a necrotizing soft-tissue infection with streptococcal toxic shock. Fluid tracking to the fascia on the first ultrasound was an early clue.

questions.q: Besides resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics, what is the most important next step?
options: MRI of the thigh to confirm fascial involvement
questions.explanation: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: early, aggressive debridement is the definitive treatment and every hour of delay raises mortality (IDSA 2014 skin and soft-tissue infection guideline). Imaging must not delay surgery in an unstable patient; hyperbaric oxygen is at most an adjunct.

questions.q: Which antibiotic should be added to suppress streptococcal toxin production?
questions.explanation: Clindamycin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and so suppresses streptococcal and staphylococcal toxin production whatever the bacterial load; IDSA recommends penicillin plus clindamycin for group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis. This patient received meropenem, vancomycin and anidulafungin; Streptococcus pyogenes was found at autopsy.

evidence.quote: This present case involves a 49-year-old female patient
admitted to the emergency department for a rash on the medial aspect of her left thigh in the context of worsening pain symptoms
Approximately 12 hours after discharge, the case was readmitted to the emergency department due to worsening of the clinical picture
in the same area and in the ipsilateral inguinal region that had started three days before the onset of the rash
swelling and reddening of the medial aspect of the left thigh and pain on palpation
extensive and marked thickening of the subcutis, with contextual, fluid stratum extending to the superficial fascial planes unharmed
The patient was given ketorolac 30 mg to relieve pain symptoms with modest benefit.
she was referred to her general practitioner
the patient reported only arterial hypertension and psoriasis
blood pressure (BP) of 110/60 mmHg, heart rate of 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 24 beats per minute
arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) of 98%
with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 15
the appearance of hemorrhagic bullous lesions on the medial side and in the inguinal area of the left thigh
the appearance of a necrotic hemorrhagic lesion on the lateral side of the ipsilateral leg (Figures 1-2) and dyspnea
C-reactive protein Increased (35.78 mg/dl)
Creatinine Increased (1.3 mg/dl)
Creatinine 2.6 mg/dl
Procalcitonin (PCT) 31.50 ng/ml
Prothrombin time (PT), INR 1.74
metabolic acidosis was found (pH, 7.23; PaCO2, 19 mmHg; HCO3, 8.0 mmol/L; Lac, 9.8 mmol/L)
The autopsy revealed the presence of S. pyogenes in the pleural and pericardial fluid.
started on antibiotic therapy with meropenem (Merrem), vancomycin and anidulafungin
About an hour after being admitted to the emergency medicine ward, the patient presented a clinical picture of septic shock
marked hypotension (65/40 mmHg)
the patient was intubated and subjected to invasive mechanical ventilation
The circulation was supported by noradrenaline in continuous infusion (0.8 micrograms/kg/min).
asystole ensued, which persisted despite the advanced cardiopulmonary resuscitation maneuvers carried out, and therefore, death was established
